title: Many at once
goal: Form the plural of the first and second declensions for all four jobs you know, and spot the neuter trap whose plural ends in -a.
bekal: turn singular nouns into plurals in all four forms
tell *templa* (temples) from *villa* (house) just by knowing its group
use *multi*, *multae*, *multa* and *pauci* in the right outfit

dialogs.title: Colloquium — Discipuli sine tabulis
dialogs.intro: Morning at Titus's school. The class is full today, but the writing tablets have been left all over the place.

lines.text: Hodie multi discipuli in schola sunt.

notes: **Three plural subject endings, one for each group.** *Discipulae* from *discipula*, *discipuli* from *discipulus*, *verba* from *verbum*. Notice that each differs from its singular only in the last letter — which is exactly why reading right to the last letter matters so much.

**Verba is plural, even though it ends in -a.** This is the biggest trap in this unit. *Villa* (ending in *-a*, group one) means "house", singular. *Verba* (from *verbum*, neuter group two) means "words", plural. What decides isn't the last letter but the word's group. If you know the dictionary form — *verbum, verbi* — you won't be fooled. English kept a few such plurals: *data*, *media*, *curricula*.

**Magistrorum, puerorum — the plural "of" form.** The ending is *-arum* for group one and *-orum* for group two. It lives on in phrases like *summa summarum* and *mater studiorum*, and in names like *Angelorum* on old church maps.

**Adsunt = ad + sunt.** Many Latin verbs are built by sticking a preposition onto another verb: *adsum* ("I'm present"), *absum* ("I'm absent"), *possum* ("I can"). They all use the *sum* endings you learned in Unit 1 — hence English *absent* and *present*.

sections.title: Plurals of the first and second declensions

blocks.text: Everything you learned in Units 3, 4 and 5 now gets its plural partner. There are no new rules — just one extra column in each table.

Notice three things. First, the *-is* form is used for every group, so *puellis* and *amicis* end the same. Second, neuter words stay true to their rule: subject and object are twins, and the plural always ends in *-a*. Third, the plural "of" form is always long and echoing — *-arum*, *-orum* — so it's the easiest to spot in a sentence.

blocks.title: Two look-alikes to watch out for
items: *puellae* can mean "of the girl" (singular "of") **or** "the girls" (plural subject). The sentence decides: if the verb is plural, so is the noun.
*amici* can mean "of the friend" **or** "the friends". Same method: check the verb.
*templa* and *villa* look alike, but *templa* is plural and *villa* is singular. Learn each word with its "of" form and the trap disappears.

sections.title: Adjectives and quantity words in the plural

blocks.text: Adjectives take exactly the same plural endings as their nouns, so there's nothing new to learn. All you need is practice pairing them.

*Multa* standing alone means "many things", and *pauca* means "few things" — Latin uses the neuter plural to talk about unnamed things. That habit gives us the phrase *cetera* you use every day in the abbreviation *etc.*: *et cetera* means "and the remaining things".

sections.title: Plural verbs and the relatives of sum

blocks.text: You've had the plural verb forms since Unit 3; only the practice is new. Three plural endings hold across all of Latin: *-mus* (we), *-tis* (you, pl), *-nt* (they).
They all use the *sum* endings you already know, so there's no new table. *Adsum!* was what a Roman pupil answered when his name was called — exactly like "Here!" or "Present!" in class today.
